_readme: content_md for Chapter 9. This is the densest chapter in the Diploma. Sassa: students will likely lean on ShalaKasi's chat heavily here more than any other chapter — worth watching the admin chat log closely after the first few students go through this one, to see where the explanations need work.

sections.9.0:
So far this Diploma has covered what Bitcoin is and how to use it. This chapter goes one level deeper: how does it actually work, under the hood?

You don't need to become a programmer to finish this chapter — but understanding these mechanics will make you a far more confident, self-sufficient Bitcoin user, and it's genuinely satisfying once it clicks.

Activity: watch "How Bitcoin Works Under the Hood" before continuing.
sections.9.1: Every Bitcoin wallet is built on a pair of mathematically linked keys: a private key (kept secret, proves ownership) and a public key (shared openly, used to receive funds). This pairing is what makes self-custody possible without needing a central authority to verify who owns what.
sections.9.1.1:
Your private key is a very large random number — effectively impossible to guess. Your public key is mathematically derived from it, but critically, the process only works in one direction: you can generate a public key from a private key easily, but you cannot reverse-engineer the private key from the public one.

This one-way relationship is what lets you safely share your public key (or an address derived from it) with anyone, while your private key stays secret and secure.
sections.9.1.2:
A hash function takes any input — a word, a file, a transaction — and produces a fixed-length string of characters that looks completely random. The same input always produces the same hash, but even a tiny change to the input produces a completely different hash, with no way to predict how.

Activity: try the Generate SHA-256 Hash exercise — type in a sentence, then change just one letter, and see how completely different the resulting hash is. This property is what makes Bitcoin's blockchain tamper-evident: changing any past transaction would change its hash, breaking the chain that follows it.
sections.9.2:
Unlike a bank account with a single running balance, Bitcoin tracks ownership through UTXOs — Unspent Transaction Outputs. Think of it less like a bank balance and more like a wallet full of individual notes of different denominations: when you spend, you use one or more whole UTXOs as inputs, and any leftover amount is sent back to yourself as 'change,' creating a new UTXO.

This model is part of what makes Bitcoin's ledger easy for anyone to independently verify — every bitcoin in existence can be traced back through an unbroken chain of UTXOs to when it was first mined.
sections.9.3: Two distinct groups of participants keep the Bitcoin network running: nodes, which verify the rules are being followed, and miners, which propose new blocks of transactions. It's worth understanding these as separate roles, even though the same computer can sometimes do both.
sections.9.3.1:
A full node downloads and independently verifies every single transaction and block against Bitcoin's rules — nobody needs to trust a node operator's word, because anyone can run their own node and check for themselves. This is what 'don't trust, verify' from Chapter 7 actually looks like in practice.

Activity: watch the video on Bitcoin nodes — running your own is more accessible than most people expect, and is a meaningful next step in Bitcoin independence once you're ready.
sections.9.3.2: Miners compete to solve the Proof-of-Work puzzle introduced in Chapter 6, using specialized hardware. Whoever solves it first proposes the next block of transactions and receives newly minted bitcoin plus transaction fees as a reward. This process also sets the network's difficulty automatically, adjusting roughly every two weeks to keep new blocks arriving about every 10 minutes regardless of how much total mining power is competing.
sections.9.4:
Before a transaction is confirmed in a block, it waits in the mempool — a holding area of pending transactions that every node maintains. When network activity is high, the mempool can back up, and transactions offering higher fees tend to get picked up by miners first.

Activity: look at a live mempool visualizer during the Mempool activity — watching real pending transactions move through in real time makes this concept concrete fast.
sections.9.5:
Bringing it all together: you sign a transaction with your private key, it's broadcast to the network and sits in the mempool, a miner includes it in a block after solving the Proof-of-Work puzzle, and every node independently verifies that block follows every rule before accepting it into their copy of the blockchain.

Every concept from this chapter — keys, hashing, UTXOs, nodes, miners, the mempool — is one link in that same single chain of events. That's Bitcoin, from click to confirmation.
